design_detail: ELEKT-D: pragmatic, open-label, randomized noninferiority trial at five US sites (a community hospital of the Cleveland Clinic, a VA hospital with Baylor College of Medicine, and Yale, Johns Hopkins and Mount Sinai), March 2017 to September 2022. 403 adults aged 21 to 75 with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant major depression referred to an ECT service were randomized 1:1 (stratified by site) to a 3-week course of intravenous ketamine twice weekly or ECT three times weekly, and were allowed to continue their existing medications. Primary outcome: response on the self-rated QIDS-SR-16 (a fall of at least 50% from the first treatment visit) at the end-of-treatment visit, within 3 days after the last session, in a modified intention-to-treat population; noninferiority margin −10 percentage points. Responders were followed for 6 months while receiving whatever treatment their own clinicians prescribed. Funded by PCORI; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03113968.
can_establish: Whether, in adults referred for ECT with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression (mostly outpatients), a 3-week course of ketamine infusions produced self-rated response at the end of treatment no more than 10 percentage points less often than a course of ECT given as specified here, and how the two courses compared on clinician-rated depression, memory tests and moderate or severe adverse events over those 3 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether ketamine works better than no active treatment or placebo (none was included); comparative effects free of expectation and preference (open label, self-rated primary outcome, 31 of 203 assigned to ECT never started it); comparison with ECT given bilaterally from the start or for more sessions; effects in psychotic depression (excluded), in inpatients (11% of the sample) or in older adults (the authors call for studies in older patients); and long-term comparative effectiveness or safety, since follow-up covered responders only, under uncontrolled treatment.

sample.recruitment: Clinic referrals: outpatients or inpatients referred by their own clinicians to the ECT service of one of five sites (an urban community hospital, a VA hospital and three university hospital centres), invited to take part, March 2017 to September 2022 (pp. 2316–2317).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 21 to 75; DSM-5 major depressive disorder without psychotic features; unsatisfactory response to at least two adequate antidepressant trials in the lifetime, verified from the referring clinician's information, Antidepressant Treatment History Form guidelines and interview; MADRS above 20; no contraindication to ketamine or ECT. The full criteria are in the protocol (p. 2317), which was not read.
sample.demographics: Mean age 46 (45.6 ketamine, 47.1 ECT); 206 of 403 (51.1%) women; 355 (88.1%) White; 359 (89.1%) outpatients at randomization; median current episode 2.0 years (IQR 0.8 to 6.0); median 5 previous episodes; 157 (39.0%) had attempted suicide; previous ECT 11.5% and 10.3%, previous ketamine 7.0% and 3.9%. Baseline MADRS 32.3 and 32.6, QIDS-SR-16 17.9 and 18.2 (Table 1, p. 2318; Results › Patients, p. 2320). Coexisting diagnoses included generalized anxiety disorder (56.5%, 55.7%), PTSD (19.0%, 24.6%), alcohol use disorder (4.0%, 5.4%) and moderate-to-severe substance use (5.0%, 6.4%).
sample.attrition: 35 did not start the assigned treatment (4 of 200 assigned ketamine, 31 of 203 assigned ECT) and 3 more had no post-treatment QIDS-SR-16 rating (1 and 2), leaving 195 and 170 in the modified intention-to-treat population (p. 2320). The authors attribute the higher withdrawal before ECT to patient preferences and logistic issues (p. 2323) and say the analysed patients were similar to those who dropped out (Table S2, supplement, not read). Of those analysed, 180 of 195 (92.3%) completed all six ketamine sessions and 158 of 170 (92.9%) completed six to nine ECT sessions (p. 2321).
sample.selection_effects: People referred for ECT who accepted randomization between ECT and ketamine; mostly White and outpatients; psychotic depression excluded. Pre-treatment withdrawal was unbalanced (2.0% against 15.3%, editors' calculation), so the analysed ECT group is the subset willing to start ECT.

exposure.measurement: Treatment delivered at the trial sites as assigned; adherence counted as sessions completed (p. 2321). ECT technique changes and ketamine dose changes are summarized in Tables S6 and S7 (supplement, not read).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously over 40 minutes (the form, racemic or single enantiomer, is not stated), twice a week for 3 weeks, with dose changes allowed if clinically indicated (kept constant in nearly all patients); ECT three times a week for 3 weeks, started as right unilateral ultrabrief pulse at six times the seizure threshold set at the first session, with later changes of settings and electrode placement allowed (switched to bilateral in 39%) (pp. 2317, 2321). Treatment could end early by the investigator's judgment or the patient's choice (p. 2317).
exposure.polysubstance: Patients in both groups were allowed to continue previously prescribed psychiatric medications, whose doses and changes were recorded: at enrolment, benzodiazepines 30.0% and 31.0%, anticonvulsants 27.0% and 25.1%, atypical antipsychotics 29.5% and 28.6%, selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors 29.0% and 36.9% (Table 1, pp. 2318–2319). Their influence on either treatment is not analysed in the article. Alcohol use disorder and moderate-to-severe substance use were recorded as coexisting diagnoses (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Active comparator: ECT as specified (right unilateral ultrabrief pulse first, three sessions a week for 3 weeks). No placebo or sham group.
comparison.matching: Randomization stratified by site; baseline characteristics similar, with small differences (Hispanic 12.0% against 5.4%, OCD 4.5% against 8.9%, PTSD 19.0% against 24.6%, previous ketamine 7.0% against 3.9%) (Table 1, p. 2318).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; treatment preference and expectations, which may differ between a novel infusion and ECT, were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same rules in both groups: existing medications could be continued and were recorded (p. 2317).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: QIDS-SR-16 (16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology, self-report, 0 to 27) response, a fall of at least 50% from the first treatment visit to the end-of-treatment visit. Secondary: MADRS (clinician-rated, 0 to 60) response; remission (QIDS-SR-16 of 5 or lower; MADRS of 10 or lower); Clinical and Patient Global Impression of Improvement (CGI-I, PGI-I); changes in QIDS-SR-16 and MADRS; Global Self-Evaluation of Memory (GSE-My, self-rated, 1 to 7) and Squire Memory Complaint Questionnaire (SMCQ, self-rated, −72 to 72) at the end of treatment; change in Hopkins Verbal Learning Test–Revised T-scores (HVLT-R, rater-administered memory test: total, delayed recall, discrimination index); 16-item Quality-of-Life Scale; Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS) on treatment days; adverse events (pp. 2317, 2319). All outcomes were measured after the 3-week course, not during an infusion, except the CADSS, which was rated on treatment days (Fig. S3, supplement, not read). Follow-up of responders at months 1, 3 and 6 (p. 2316).
outcomes.validity_norms: QIDS-SR-16 described as validated and used in large depression trials (p. 2317); HVLT-R scored as T-scores with age-corrected norms (Table 2 footnote, p. 2322).
outcomes.operationalization: Response and remission as above, measured at the end-of-treatment visit within 3 days after the last session. Relapse during follow-up: QIDS-SR-16 above 11 (p. 2323). Memory harm: the end-of-treatment change in HVLT-R T-scores and the self-rated memory scales.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for secondary outcomes: the article states that their confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiplicity and may not be used in place of hypothesis testing (pp. 2319, 2322). 16 counts the primary outcome and the 15 secondary estimates in the text and Table 2; the Supplementary Appendix lists further outcomes and subgroup analyses (Table S3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. Patients, attending physicians and research staff knew the assignments (p. 2317); the primary outcome is self-rated, and the MADRS and HVLT-R were rated or administered by staff aware of the assignment.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: QIDS-SR-16 response 108/195 (55.4%) with ketamine against 70/170 (41.2%) with ECT, difference 14.2 percentage points (95% CI 3.9 to 24.2), Farrington–Manning statistic 4.64, P<0.001 for noninferiority; intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis with multiple imputation 55.4% against 41.6%, difference 13.8 (3.9 to 23.8) (p. 2320; Table 2, p. 2322). MADRS response 50.8% against 41.4%, 9.3 (−0.9 to 19.4); remission QIDS-SR-16 32.3% against 20.0%, 12.3 (3.4 to 21.2); MADRS 37.9% against 21.8%, 16.2 (7.0 to 25.4). Least-squares mean change QIDS-SR-16 −9.0 against −7.2, difference −1.8 (−2.8 to −0.8); MADRS −15.3 against −13.1, difference −2.2 (−4.1 to −0.3). HVLT-R delayed-recall T-score change −0.9 against −9.7, difference 8.8 (5.7 to 11.9) (pp. 2320, 2322). Editors' calculations: the QIDS-SR-16 change difference is about 0.4 of the baseline SD and the MADRS change difference about 0.4 of its baseline SD; number needed to treat for one additional QIDS-SR-16 response about 7.
analysis.covariates: The mixed model for repeated QIDS-SR-16 scores included treatment, assessment, their interaction and site, with a random intercept per patient (p. 2319). The response analysis is unadjusted apart from site stratification.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03113968 (p. 2315); protocol with the statistical analysis plan published with the article at NEJM.org (p. 2316). Neither the registry record nor the protocol was read for this card, so the match between the registered and reported primary outcome and margin is not verified here; the Methods and the abstract give the same primary outcome and margin.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's statement that ketamine was associated with dissociation rests on a supplementary figure (Fig. S3) with no CADSS values in the article; adverse events in the article are moderate and severe events only (full list in Table S8); relapse percentages are given without denominators (Table S9). Subgroup results are in Table S3 only.
analysis.power: Powered for noninferiority: 346 participants for 80% power (one-sided alpha 0.025), margin −10 percentage points, assuming 50% response to ECT and a true difference of 5 percentage points; 400 planned to allow 15% attrition (p. 2319). Observed ECT response (41.2%) was below the assumed 50%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 365 analysed patients referred for ECT, self-rated response at the end of a 3-week course was 55.4% after ketamine and 41.2% after ECT, so the prespecified noninferiority test was met by a wide margin (lower limit 3.9 against a margin of −10); clinician-rated response did not differ significantly (9.3 points, −0.9 to 19.4), while remission rates and change scores favoured ketamine by small to moderate amounts. ECT was followed by a larger fall in verbal memory test scores at the end of treatment; among responders followed up, scores had returned to similar levels by 1 month. More patients assigned to ECT withdrew before starting it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that ketamine was noninferior to ECT for treatment-resistant depression without psychosis, and that ECT was associated with musculoskeletal adverse effects and ketamine with dissociation (p. 2315). This matches the prespecified analysis. Gaps: (1) the abstract says ketamine was administered to 195 and ECT to 170 patients after 38 withdrew before treatment, whereas the Results show 35 never started and 3 started without a post-treatment rating (p. 2320); (2) the abstract does not mention that the trial was open-label with a self-rated primary outcome, or that ECT response (41.2%) was lower than the 50% assumed in the power calculation and than other reports, which the Discussion attributes partly to starting with right unilateral placement in mostly outpatients (p. 2324); (3) the dissociation statement has no numbers in the article. The Discussion names open-label design, the lack of placebo, flexible treatment and uncontrolled follow-up as limitations (p. 2324) and limits the conclusion to nonpsychotic depression.

timeline.event: Berman et al.: an early placebo-controlled report (by its authors' account the first) of lower depression ratings after one ketamine infusion (7 completers); Amit Anand, first author of this trial, is a co-author.

Murrough et al.: two-site trial of one ketamine infusion against midazolam as an active placebo (as recorded on this round's first-pass card sc_murrough_2013); James W. Murrough is an author of both trials.

KetECT, a European open-label noninferiority trial of racemic ketamine against ECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022), and a meta-analysis of ketamine against ECT (Rhee et al., 2022) found remission with ketamine inferior to ECT, as described in this article's Discussion (p. 2323; neither read).
This trial: noninferiority of ketamine to ECT on self-rated response in 365 analysed patients with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression.

replication.where_it_stands: The two large randomized comparisons of ketamine and ECT point in different directions on remission: the earlier European trial and a meta-analysis (as described here) favoured ECT, this trial favoured or matched ketamine. The authors attribute the difference to the exclusion of psychotic depression, a larger and mostly outpatient sample and an ECT protocol that started with right unilateral placement (pp. 2323–2324). The question of which treatment is better for whom stays open.

funding.funder: Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI), under a contract with the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, named as the sponsor (p. 2316); supported by an award (TRD-1511-33648, to Dr. Anand) from PCORI (p. 2324). The article states that the views are the authors' alone and not necessarily PCORI's (p. 2324).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not printed in the article: disclosure forms are available with the full text at NEJM.org (p. 2324) and were not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Designed and supervised by an executive committee of the first author and the site principal investigators; data coordination and project management by the Cleveland Clinic Center for Clinical Research; statistical analysis by the last author (Cleveland Clinic); first author wrote the manuscript; a data and safety monitoring board and a stakeholder committee oversaw the trial (pp. 2316–2317). No industry funder is named. Several authors are investigators of earlier ketamine trials: Anand is an author of Berman et al. (2000), and Murrough and Mathew of Murrough et al. (2013) (author lists in the reference records). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of ketamine and ECT with a clinician-rated primary outcome scored by raters unaware of the assignment, an ECT protocol at full strength (with a prespecified switch to bilateral placement or more sessions), enrolment of inpatients and older adults, and randomized continuation treatment with relapse over 6 to 12 months as an outcome.

domains.note: Randomization through a secure electronic data-management system, stratified by site (p. 2317), which implies concealed allocation; baseline characteristics similar apart from small differences (Table 1).

Open label for patients, physicians and staff. 31 of 203 assigned to ECT never started it (against 4 of 200 for ketamine), which the authors attribute to preferences and logistics; ECT technique was changed to bilateral in 39% and treatment could stop early; concomitant medications were allowed. The primary analysis excluded those who did not start (modified intention to treat), but an intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation gave the same result.

38 of 403 (9.4%) lack the primary outcome, unevenly (5 of 200 against 33 of 203; editors' calculation); several imputation scenarios supported noninferiority, and the authors report that analysed patients resembled dropouts (Table S2, supplement, not read).

The primary outcome is self-rated by patients who knew which treatment they received, in a comparison where preferences and logistics stopped 15% of those assigned to ECT from starting it; the clinician-rated MADRS and the HVLT-R were scored by staff aware of the assignment. The authors say the open-label design could have influenced response (p. 2324).

Registered, with protocol and analysis plan published alongside; the Methods' primary outcome and margin match the abstract, but neither the registry nor the protocol was read for this card. Secondary estimates are reported without multiplicity adjustment, as stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Allocation was sound and the noninferiority result held in intention-to-treat sensitivity analyses, so random error and attrition are unlikely to explain it. The overall judgment is high because the primary outcome is self-rated in an open-label comparison between treatments that patients view very differently, as the uneven withdrawal before ECT shows; expectation could favour either arm, and its direction cannot be known. The ECT comparator, started as right unilateral ultrabrief pulse in mostly outpatients, produced a lower response than the authors assumed, which affects how far the result generalizes rather than its internal validity. The source can be cited for noninferiority of a 3-week ketamine course to ECT given this way on self-rated response, for the remission and memory-test differences at the end of treatment, and for moderate and severe adverse event rates; it cannot be cited for comparisons with bilateral or longer ECT, for psychotic or late-life depression, for dissociation magnitudes, or for comparative relapse, which comes from uncontrolled follow-up of responders.

key_findings.finding: Open-label, randomized noninferiority trial at five US sites (one community hospital, one VA hospital, three university centres); patients, attending physicians and research staff knew the assignment; randomization 1:1 through a secure electronic system, stratified by site.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial Design and Oversight, 1st paragraph (p. 2316); Methods › Randomization and Treatment, 1st paragraph (p. 2317)

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously over 40 minutes, twice a week for 3 weeks (dose modification allowed if clinically indicated), against ECT three times a week for 3 weeks, started as right unilateral ultrabrief pulse at six times the seizure threshold with later changes allowed; patients in both groups were allowed to continue their previously prescribed medications.

Eligibility: age 21 to 75, DSM-5 major depressive disorder without psychotic features, unsatisfactory response to at least two adequate antidepressant trials, MADRS above 20, referred to an ECT service, March 2017 to September 2022.

403 were randomized (200 ketamine, 203 ECT); 35 did not start treatment (4 ketamine, 31 ECT) and 3 had no post-treatment QIDS-SR-16 rating (1 and 2), leaving 365 in the modified intention-to-treat population (195 and 170).

Sample: mean age 46, 206 (51.1%) women, 355 (88.1%) White, 359 (89.1%) outpatients; median current episode 2.0 years; 157 (39.0%) had attempted suicide; baseline MADRS 32.3 (SD 6.2) and 32.6 (SD 6.0), QIDS-SR-16 17.9 (SD 4.1) and 18.2 (SD 4.2); previous ketamine treatment 14 (7.0%) and 8 (3.9%).

Primary outcome: QIDS-SR-16 response at the end-of-treatment visit in 108 of 195 (55.4%) after ketamine and 70 of 170 (41.2%) after ECT, difference 14.2 percentage points (95% CI 3.9 to 24.2; Farrington–Manning statistic 4.64; P<0.001 for noninferiority, margin −10). Intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation: 55.4% against 41.6%, difference 13.8 (3.9 to 23.8).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary Outcome (p. 2320); Table 2, primary outcome row (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: Clinician-rated MADRS response: 99 of 195 (50.8%) against 70 of 169 (41.4%), difference 9.3 percentage points (95% CI −0.9 to 19.4). Least-squares mean change from baseline: QIDS-SR-16 −9.0 against −7.2 (difference −1.8, 95% CI −2.8 to −0.8); MADRS −15.3 against −13.1 (difference −2.2, 95% CI −4.1 to −0.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Depression, 1st paragraph (p. 2320); Table 2 (p. 2322)
key_findings.note: Secondary outcome; the article states that its confidence intervals are not adjusted for multiplicity and may not be used in place of hypothesis testing.

key_findings.finding: Remission: QIDS-SR-16 score of 5 or lower in 63 of 195 (32.3%) against 34 of 170 (20.0%), difference 12.3 (95% CI 3.4 to 21.2); MADRS of 10 or lower in 74 of 195 (37.9%) against 37 of 170 (21.8%), difference 16.2 (7.0 to 25.4).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Depression, 2nd paragraph (p. 2320); Table 2 (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: Global improvement: CGI-I much improved or better 99/189 (52.4%) against 78/164 (47.6%), 4.8 (−5.6 to 15.3); very much improved 59/189 (31.2%) against 35/164 (21.3%), 9.9 (0.8 to 19.0). PGI-I much improved or better 84/190 (44.2%) against 60/164 (36.6%), 7.6 (−2.6 to 17.8); very much improved 37/190 (19.5%) against 18/164 (11.0%), 8.5 (1.1 to 15.9).
key_findings.note: The footnote's threshold for 'much improved or better' is misprinted; see reporting issue 2.

key_findings.finding: Memory at the end of treatment: change in HVLT-R delayed-recall T-score −0.9 (SE 1.1) after ketamine against −9.7 (SE 1.2) after ECT, difference 8.8 (95% CI 5.7 to 11.9); total 3.2 against −2.1, difference 5.3 (3.1 to 7.4); discrimination index −1.5 against −9.7, difference 8.2 (5.2 to 11.3). Self-rated memory: GSE-My 4.2 against 3.2 (difference 1.1, 0.9 to 1.2); SMCQ 0.2 against −8.8 (difference 9.0, 5.1 to 13.0).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Cognitive Impairment and Quality of Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2320); Table 2 (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: Among ECT responders, HVLT-R scores that were lower than in the ketamine group at the end of treatment had returned to similar levels by the 1-month visit and stayed stable to 6 months; SMCQ scores recovered gradually, while GSE-My scores remained lower than in the ketamine group through the end of follow-up.
key_findings.note: Values are in Table S9 (supplement, not read).

key_findings.finding: Quality of life (16-item scale) rose by 12.3 points after ketamine and 12.9 after ECT, difference −0.6 (95% CI −3.4 to 2.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Cognitive Impairment and Quality of Life, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 2320, the quality-of-life sentences at the top of p. 2321, left column); Table 2 (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: 180 of 195 (92.3%) completed all six ketamine sessions and 158 of 170 (92.9%) completed six to nine ECT sessions; ECT was changed from right unilateral to bilateral in 39% of patients, and the ketamine dose was kept constant in nearly all.

Moderate or severe adverse events in the 3-week phase: at least one in 49 of 195 (25.1%) with ketamine against 55 of 170 (32.4%) with ECT; muscle pain or weakness 1/195 (0.5%) against 9/170 (5.3%), P = 0.01; gastrointestinal 6.7% against 5.3%; headache 8.2% against 7.1%; severe or prolonged hypertension 6/195 (3.1%) against 4/170 (2.4%); new suicidal ideation 4/195 (2.1%) against 2/170 (1.2%); no suicide attempts; no deaths during the trial. P>0.05 for all except muscle pain or weakness.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events; Table 3, initial treatment phase
key_findings.note: Table 3 lists moderate and severe events only; the full adverse-event list is in Table S8 (supplement, not read).

key_findings.finding: Dissociative symptoms (CADSS) were higher in the ketamine group than in the ECT group on all treatment days; no values are given in the article.
key_findings.note: The data are in Fig. S3 of the supplement, not read.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up of responders, treated as their own clinicians prescribed: relapse (QIDS-SR-16 above 11) in 19.0% after ketamine against 35.4% after ECT at month 1, 25.0% against 50.9% at month 3 and 34.5% against 56.3% at month 6. During follow-up, at least one moderate or severe adverse event in 17/108 (15.7%) against 10/70 (14.3%); suicidal ideation 4/108 (3.7%) against 1/70 (1.4%); one suicide attempt (1/108) in the ketamine group.
key_findings.note: Relapse denominators and the treatments received during follow-up are in Tables S9 and S10 (supplement, not read); the comparison is no longer randomized, because it is restricted to responders and follow-up treatment was not controlled.

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations that ECT started with right unilateral placement and might have produced more responses if started bilaterally or given for more sessions, that the open-label design could have influenced response, that maintenance treatment was not studied, and the lack of placebo; they note their ECT response and remission rates were lower than in other reports, resembling community and outpatient settings.

The authors state that their results differ from those of a recent European trial (KetECT) and a meta-analysis, in which remission with ketamine was inferior to ECT, and attribute this to the exclusion of psychotic depression, a larger sample and a mostly outpatient population (89%).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 2323, right column, continued on p. 2324)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that after 38 patients withdrew before starting the assigned treatment, ketamine was given to 195 patients and ECT to 170. The Results say 35 did not start (4 and 31) and 3 started but had no post-treatment rating; 195 and 170 are the modified intention-to-treat counts. Editors' arithmetic from p. 2320: 196 started ketamine and 172 started ECT.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but claims should use the Results' flow (35 never started, 31 of them assigned to ECT).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 2 footnotes define a CGI-I or PGI-I rating of 'much improved or better' as a score lower than 2, which on a 1-to-7 scale is a score of 1, the same as 'very much improved'; the table gives different counts for the two (99 against 59 for CGI-I with ketamine).
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold must have been 2 or lower; a typographical error in the footnote, without effect on the numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Table 2 footnote give the range of HVLT-R delayed-recall and discrimination-index T-scores as −300 to 200, which is not the range of a T-score (a metric with mean 50 and SD 10); the footnote adds that age-corrected norms were used.
reporting_issues.consequence: The metric in which the 8.8-point delayed-recall difference is expressed is unclear; claims should give the difference without converting it into standard deviations.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that ketamine was associated with dissociation, but the article gives no CADSS values, only a reference to a supplementary figure; Table 3 lists moderate and severe adverse events only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and duration of dissociation, and the frequency of mild adverse events, cannot be cited from the article itself.

reporting_issues.issue: Relapse percentages during follow-up are printed without denominators, and the follow-up compares responders under treatments chosen by their own clinicians.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower relapse after ketamine (34.5% against 56.3% at month 6) is not a randomized comparison and cannot be cited as one.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Anand_2023_KetamineVsECT.pdf: printed pp. 2315–2325, the final issue version (June 22, 2023; first published May 24, 2023): abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 3 and Figure 1 checked on the rendered pages (150 dpi), funding, appendix and references. Not read: the Supplementary Appendix (Tables S1 to S10, Figs. S1 to S4), the protocol and statistical analysis plan, the disclosure forms and the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT03113968. Findings that depend on the supplement are marked.
